```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
```

## Airbnb Example

```{r}
data("nyc_airbnb")

nyc_airbnb = 
  nyc_airbnb |> 
  mutate(
    stars = review_scores_location / 2                     # converts the 0-10 location score to a 0-5 star scale
  ) |> 
  rename(                                                  # rename(new_name = old_name)
    borough = neighbourhood_group,
    neighborhood = neighbourhood
  ) |> 
  filter(
    borough != "Staten Island"                             # drops Staten Island (due to its very few listings)
  ) |> 
  select(price, stars, borough, neighborhood, room_type)   # keeps only the variables used in the models
```

Fit a Linear Regression

```{r}
# `lm(outcome ~ predictor1 + predictor2, data = ...)`: price as a function of stars and borough.
# borough is categorical, so R creates an indicator (dummy) variable for each borough,
# compared against a reference category: the first level alphabetically, here the Bronx

fit = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb)
```

Look at the Results

```{r}
fit                   # coefficients only
summary(fit)          # coefficients, standard errors, t-statistics, p-values, R-squared
coef(fit)             # just the coefficient estimates, as a named vector
fitted.values(fit)    # predicted price for every listing (prints all ~40,000)
resid(fit)            # residuals: observed price minus predicted price

names(fit)            # the components stored inside the model object
names(summary(fit))   # components of the summary (e.g., r.squared), which you can pull out individually
```

Most of this Output is Bad; Let's Use Broom

```{r}
# `broom::tidy()` turns the coefficient table into a tidy dataframe (one row per term), so it can be filtered, mutated, and formatted like any other data

broom::tidy(fit) |>
  select(-std.error) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

broom::glance(fit)    # one-row summary of overall model fit: R-squared, AIC, number of observations, etc.
```

Change the Reference Category

```{r}
fit =
  nyc_airbnb |>
  mutate(
    borough = fct_infreq(borough)         # reorders levels by frequency, so the most common borough (Manhattan) becomes the reference
  ) |>
  lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = _)   # `_` is the native pipe placeholder: lm()'s first argument is the formula, so `data = _` tells the pipe where to send the data

broom::tidy(fit) |>
  select(-std.error, -statistic) |>
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough: ")) |>   # readable labels: "boroughBrooklyn" becomes "Borough: Brooklyn"
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Diagnostics

Diagnostics efers to analyzing the residuals

```{r}
modelr::add_residuals(nyc_airbnb, fit)   # adds a `resid` column (observed - predicted price) to the data
```


```{r}
nyc_airbnb |>                               # residuals vs. stars: spread isn't constant, and a few very high prices skew it
  modelr::add_residuals(fit) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stars, y = resid)) +
  geom_point()

nyc_airbnb |>                               # residuals by borough: long upper tails, so residuals aren't normal or constant
  modelr::add_residuals(fit) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = borough, y = resid)) +
  geom_violin()
```

## Hypothesis Testing

```{r}
# the p.value column tests whether each coefficient differs from 0 (a t-test for each term)

broom::tidy(fit) |>
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough: ")) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Try Testing Nested Models

```{r}
# Nested models: the null model is the alternative model with some terms removed. `anova()` runs an F-test of whether adding borough (all of its indicator terms at once) significantly improves the fit, which a single coefficient's p-value can't tell you

fit_null = lm(price ~ stars, data = nyc_airbnb)
fit_alt = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb)

anova(fit_null, fit_alt)
```

## Nesting Data

Trying More Complicated Models

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |>
  lm(price ~ stars * borough + room_type * borough, data = _) |> # `*` adds main effects and interactions: tests whether the effect of stars on price, and the effect of room type, differ by borough
  broom::tidy() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Determining What's Happening in Manhattan

```{r}
# The same model fit separately within one borough at a time

nyc_airbnb |>
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |>
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = _) |>
  broom::tidy()

nyc_airbnb |>
  filter(borough == "Bronx") |>
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = _) |>
  broom::tidy()
```

Let's Fix This With Iteration

```{r}
# Wrapping the model in a function lets map() apply it to many datasets

airbnb_lm = function(data) {

  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = data)
  
}
```

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |>
  nest(datasets = -borough) |>          # one row per borough; `datasets` is a list column holding that borough's data
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, airbnb_lm),    # fits the model to each borough's data
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)    # tidies up the results of each linear model fit
  ) |>
  select(-datasets, -fits) |>           # drops the list columns that are no longer needed
  unnest(results) |>                    # expands the tidy tables: one row per borough x term
  select(borough, term, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(                          # one column per term, to compare coefficients across boroughs
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  )
```

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |>
  nest(datasets = -borough) |>
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, \(data) lm(price ~ stars, data = data)), # `\(data)` is shorthand for function(data): an anonymous function written in place
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |>
  select(-datasets, -fits) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  select(borough, term, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  )
```

```{r}
# Same approach within Manhattan, with one model per neighborhood. The plot shows how the price difference for a private room (vs. an entire home/apt) varies across neighborhoods

nyc_airbnb |>
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |>
  nest(datasets = -neighborhood) |>
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, \(df) lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = df)),
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |>
  select(neighborhood, results) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  filter(term == "room_typePrivate room") |>                    # keeps only the private room coefficient
  ggplot(aes(x = neighborhood, y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 80, hjust = 1))      # rotates neighborhood labels so they don't overlap
```

## Logistic Regression

Importing the WP Homicide Data

```{r}
baltimore_df = 
  read_csv("data/homicide-data.csv") |>
  filter(city == "Baltimore") |>
  mutate(
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),   # binary outcome: 1 if solved by arrest, 0 otherwise
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)                         # "Unknown" ages become NA (a warning here is expected)
  )
```

Fit the Logistic Regression

```{r}
fit_logistic = 
  baltimore_df |>
  mutate(victim_race = fct_infreq(victim_race)) |>                          # most common race becomes the reference category
  glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_race, data = _, family = binomial())   # `glm()` with family = `binomial()` fits a logistic regression

fit_logistic |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  mutate(OR = exp(estimate)) |>               # coefficients are on the log-odds scale; `exp()` converts them to odds ratios
  select(term, OR, estimate, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
